A simple but meaningful event was underway: the Curhat Cinta Istana Podcast, initiated by Nisa and Reza. That podcast, initially considered a casual side project, unexpectedly exploded into a national phenomenon. Nisa's calming voice, combined with Reza's witty but empathetic remarks, turned out to be the balm needed by millions of ears throughout the country. They discussed issues around marriage, parenting, to daily life pressure in down-to-earth, honest, non-judgmental language. This podcast's success was what drove Nisa to create a physical space within the Palace grounds for staff and their families to share stories and get support.

Today, Nisa, dressed in a brightly colored, unpretentious Sumba woven blouse, looked so free. She crouched, matching the height of a shy little girl who was the daughter of one of the Palace's cleaning staff, listening to her chatter attentively. Reza, standing not far from her, was engaged in casual chat with several young fathers from the presidential guard corps, sharing tips — or perhaps complaints — about staying up late with a baby. That scene was so contrasting with the gripping tension in the Situation Room or the plenary session months ago.

This was the sweet fruit of their bitter struggle. The passage of the Family Readiness Bill, though through a steep path full of slander and fierce resistance, was now slowly showing its positive impact. The number of underage marriage dispensation applications was reported to have declined significantly in several pilot regions. The modernized and mandatory premarital course began getting appreciation for its relevant, applicable material. Though resistance from conservative groups hadn't fully died down, public narrative slowly shifted toward acceptance, driven by real testimonies from young couples feeling the benefit of more mature preparation.

Nisa Farha's popularity as president skyrocketed to a level never seen before. She was no longer just seen as a smart technocrat or tough politician, but also as the “Mother of the Nation” caring for the country's smallest foundation: family. Latest public opinion surveys consistently showed extraordinary support for Nisa to run again for a second term. The hashtag #NisaLagiUntukIndonesia often dominated social media conversation, far outdoing negative hashtags once trying to bring her down. This euphoria of support felt so real, warm, and promising a smooth path toward the next contest.

Amid that small crowd, Angel Marina and Anton Prasetya stood side by side, watching Nisa and Reza with relieved smiles. The heavy burden they'd carried together during the previous Bill crisis now felt lighter.

“I can hardly believe we made it to this point, Anton,” Angel whispered quietly, her eyes still fixed on Nisa now laughing with the Palace staff mothers. “It feels like… just yesterday we were all nearly going crazy from that slander storm.”

Anton Prasetya nodded, adjusting his glasses. “The President's hard work, the team's solidity, and… maybe a little miracle from public support,” he answered analytically as usual, but there was warmth in his tone. “But… we mustn't be complacent, Angel. This honeymoon period won't last forever. The next election draws closer, political opponents surely won't stay idle.”
Angel sighed. “You're right. I just hope… this time it's not as brutal as before.”

Elsewhere, in the heart of Jakarta's glittering business district, in a luxurious dark-glass-walled meeting room on a skyscraper's highest floor, the atmosphere felt far different. Cold air conditioning air felt piercing, silent, only broken by the clink of glasses holding expensive drinks or a hoarse voice full of disappointment.

Hardiman Suryo, the veteran senior politician who was the main driver of resistance against the Family Readiness Bill, sat leaning back in his luxurious leather chair. His usually slick, cynically smiling face now looked rigid holding back anger. Before him sat several other key figures: an influential senior media businessman whose news portal actively 'fried' negative issues about Nisa, who still had strong networks in several lines, and a highly paid political consultant known for his 'scorched earth' strategy.

“Her popularity keeps rising,” hissed the media businessman, roughly setting down his tablet displaying the latest survey data onto the table. “That damn podcast, the Family Bill starting to be accepted… That woman really knows how to win the common people's hearts.”

“We failed to stop the bill in parliament,” added the general in a heavy tone. “The campaign fund slander attack we designed with such difficulty was neutralized just like that by that irrational public support.”

Hardiman Suryo tapped his fat fingers on the shiny wooden table surface, his eyes staring blankly at the city view outside the glass window. The defeat at the plenary session months ago still burned his pride. He felt humiliated, not only by Nisa Farha, but also by the wave of 'ordinary people's' support that succeeded in turning the tide.

“We focused too much on attacking the bill,” Hardiman finally said, his voice hoarse and cold. “We underestimated her ability to build a narrative as 'protector of families.' Now, her image is too strong to attack directly on her policy.”

The political consultant, a dapper man in his forties with a thin, unreadable smile, leaned forward. “If we can't attack her fortress from the front, we have to find a gap from the side… or from within,” he said quietly, full of meaning.
Hardiman's eyes gleamed. “Meaning?”

“Nisa Farha might seem perfect now,” the consultant continued. “But no human is truly without flaw. Everyone has a weak point. Her husband, for instance. Reza Satria. Successful businessman, clean image, public's ideal husband.” He smiled cynically. “But what if we scratch that image a little? We create a narrative that his business success isn't entirely clean? That there's a 'catch' in every one of his steps? That the potential of Nisa's second term is a guarantee of favors for his projects?”

The media businessman immediately caught the direction of the conversation. “Interesting…. Conflict of interest issues are always sexy. Especially if it involves the Palace's inner circle. We could start digging up Reza Satria Group's old projects again, looking for any small potential irregularity, then blowing it up.”

“Exactly,” the consultant nodded. “First target: Reza Satria. We make the public doubt his integrity. Doubt about Reza will automatically spread to Nisa. After that…,” he paused briefly, letting his plan hang. “…we look at the next weakness. Maybe… their son? Alex, if I'm not mistaken? Young people are usually easier to 'play.'”

Hardiman Suryo smiled thinly for the first time that night. A cold, calculating smile. “I like the direction,” he murmured. “Destroy her support foundation one by one. Make her isolated, busy handling her own family's internal problems. Let her feel what it's like when her world collapses from within.”

A new threat began being woven in that luxurious meeting room's silence. Seeds of intrigue far more personal and cruel began being planted, waiting for the right time to grow and trap the president in a different storm, a storm attacking straight at the heart of her life.

That night, in the Palace's quiet private pavilion, far from spotlight and intrigue, Nisa and Reza enjoyed a rare moment together. After putting their youngest child to sleep, they sat side by side on the balcony facing the garden, accompanied by two cups of warm tea and the peaceful night silence.
Nisa rested her head on Reza's shoulder, feeling the familiar warmth and strength of her husband. The fatigue after a day of activity began to be felt, but this time it was a satisfying fatigue.
“A beautiful day, wasn't it, Mas,” Nisa whispered quietly. “Seeing the children's and staff's smiles earlier… It feels like all yesterday's struggle meant something.”

Reza smiled, gently stroking Nisa's arm. “Of course it meant something. You've done something extraordinary, love,” he answered sincerely. He looked at the night sky beginning to be decorated with stars. “But Anton was right earlier. We mustn't be complacent. The real battle, the battle for a second term, is only about to begin.”

Nisa nodded, she was well aware of that. Today's euphoria was a precious pause, but not the journey's end. “I know,” she replied. “And I'm ready. Whatever they'll throw later, new slander, personal attacks… I won't waver. As long as you're by my side like this.”

Reza turned, gazing deep into Nisa's eyes reflecting starlight. He saw again the flame of resolve never extinguished there, the same flame that made him fall in love over a decade ago, a flame now forged even stronger by storms.
“Always,” Reza answered briefly, but heavy with meaning. He pulled Nisa closer, embracing her tightly in the night's silence. “We face it together, whatever it is.”

Under a scattering of stars, on the Palace balcony that had silently witnessed their fragility and strength, Nisa and Reza reaffirmed their promise. A promise to protect each other, strengthen each other, facing the new chapter of struggle stretched ahead. They knew the road wouldn't be easy, new threats surely lurking in the shadows. However, that night, at least for that night, they let themselves sink into the moment's peace, saving energy for the next storm quietly beginning to gather its dark clouds on the horizon. The light after the storm indeed felt warm, but the shadow of new intrigue had already begun creeping without them fully realizing it. ________________________________________________
5: A Few Weeks After the “Euphoria”
Jakarta

That post-storm calm, as anticipated by Anton Prasetya and Angel Marina, indeed didn't last long. The political wheel kept turning, and with the election year drawing closer, intrigue machines began being reactivated by those feeling threatened by Nisa Farha's continuously rising popularity. This time, the attack came from a different direction, more personal, targeting a point they considered one of Nisa's pillars of strength: Reza Satria.

Everything started again from faktaindonesia.com, the same online news portal that had once been the main mouthpiece for rejecting the Family Readiness Bill. An opinion article, again written by an “independent political observer” without a clear track record, appeared on their site's front page. Its title was provocative, designed to immediately plant seeds of doubt: “Nisa's Second Term: A Red Carpet Guarantee for the Satria Business Empire?”

That article contained no direct corruption accusation, but a series of Reza Satria Group business facts twisted and presented with a narrative full of insinuation. Reza Satria Group's rapid growth over the past five years, the solar electrification project in hundreds of remote (3T) villages in East Nusa Tenggara and Maluku — won through open tender because Reza Satria Group was the only domestic company with off-grid solar microgrid technology tested for remote archipelagic geographic conditions, and evaluated by an independent due diligence panel deliberately involved precisely because of the sensitivity of his position as the president's husband — was now twisted as if evidence of conflict of interest. The article didn't even mention the fact that since Nisa's inauguration, Reza had handed over all daily operational control of his company to an independent board of directors, a step he'd once openly been proud of. But now, along with that expansion into the green energy sector, everything was framed as if the result of conflict of interest and abuse of Nisa Farha's power. Its closing question stung: would Nisa's second term become an arena for perpetuating a family business dynasty at the heart of power? Reza read that article with a furrowed brow while having breakfast with Nisa in their private pavilion. His steaming hot coffee felt cold in his throat.
“They're starting again, love,” Reza murmured flatly, showing his tablet screen to Nisa.

Nisa read that article quickly, her jaw hardening holding back anger. The same pattern, the same strategy: attack her closest person to damage her image. “Cheap slander,” Nisa hissed. “All those projects were obtained professionally, Mas. The public knows that too.”

“The public knows, Nisa. But public opinion is very easily shaped,” Reza replied, a tired tone slipping into his voice. “This article is just the opener. Soon there'll surely be 'leaked' fake data, buzzer attacks…. They want to create a negative perception of me, and that will impact you.”
Nisa gripped her husband's hand. “We face this together. Don't let them affect you. Your business is clean, everyone knows your integrity.”
Reza returned that grip, trying to draw strength from Nisa's confident gaze. But he knew, the storm had just begun.

Sure enough, within days, that conflict-of-interest issue was thoroughly 'fried.' Other opposition news portals joined in quoting and expanding faktaindonesia.com's narrative. Hardiman Suryo and several other opposition politicians began speaking up in media, voicing 'concern' and 'the need for transparency' about the President's family business relations with state policy. The hashtag #KonflikKepentinganIstana (#PalaceConflictOfInterest) began being raised by anonymous social media accounts, spreading data fragments and baseless accusations.

Reza began feeling the impact. Several important meetings with foreign investors had to be postponed. Suspicious-toned questions began emerging from his business colleagues. He had to spend extra time explaining and clarifying, something draining his energy and focus from his actual business development. Stress began shadowing his days, though he tried hard to hide it from Nisa.
Amid this initial pressure, Nisa felt the need to share her burden with someone she trusted outside the Palace circle that now felt tense too. She contacted Dinda Larasati, her friend since college.
“Sar, have you seen the news about Mas Reza?” Nisa asked directly once their video call connected that afternoon. Nisa was in her office, trying to finish several ministerial dispositions.

On the laptop screen, Dinda's face instantly showed a shocked and truly concerned expression. “Oh my god, Nis…, yes, I saw it briefly this morning on a news portal. They're crazy! How cruel to slander Mas Reza like that! This is clearly a cheap political attack to bring you down, right?” Dinda's voice sounded equally furious, full of empathy for her friend.

Nisa sighed with relief hearing Dinda's response. Her friend was indeed always reliable. “Yes, Sar. The pattern is the same as before. Attack my closest person. Mas Reza is very stressed, even though he tries to hide it. I can't bear to see it.”

“Oh dear, poor Mas Reza,” Dinda said again, her eyes conveying deep concern. “Be patient, Nis. Stay strong! Don't let yourself fall too because of this attack. Mas Reza needs you to stay steady. I'm sure you two can get through this. You're my role-model power couple!” Dinda tried to encourage with her usual warm smile.

“Thanks, Sar. You're truly the best friend,” Nisa said, feeling a little lighter after sharing her burden. Dinda's sincere support felt like a fresh breeze. “You're welcome, Nis! Whenever you need someone to talk to, just call me. Or if you want a nice coffee outing outside the Palace to unwind, just let me know, I'm ready to accompany you! Don't hesitate!” Dinda offered again, full of warmth.

“Definitely, Sar. Thanks so much,” Nisa closed, feeling grateful to have a friend like Dinda amid this difficult situation. There wasn't the slightest doubt in Nisa's mind about Dinda's sincerity. To her, Dinda was an anchor of true friendship outside the whirlwind of politics and family.
Meanwhile, at the Situation Room, Angel and Anton began gathering data to refute the slander against Reza.

“We're preparing all Reza Satria Group's tender data and financial reports for the past five years, Ton,” Angel instructed. “We have to be able to show the public there's no anomaly or special treatment whatsoever.”

Anton nodded. “Ready, Mbak Angel. The legal team is also preparing official clarification material. But we have to be careful, mustn't seem like the Palace is too defensive of the President's family business interest.”

They were well aware, this was just the opening attack. Nisa's political opponents clearly wouldn't stop here. They had to prepare to face the next wave of attack that might be far bigger and more personal.
That night, Reza came home later than usual. He found Nisa still awake, waiting for him in the family room while reading a book. Seeing her husband's tired face, Nisa rose to approach him.
“Have you eaten, Mas?” she asked gently while helping Reza loosen his tie.
Reza shook his head slowly, letting Nisa help him. Nisa's gentle touch felt calming. “Haven't had the chance. Meetings nonstop since afternoon.” “Shall I prepare dinner?” Nisa offered.

Reza smiled tiredly, pulling Nisa into his embrace. “No need, love. I just need this.” He hugged Nisa tightly, breathing in his wife's familiar scent. In Nisa's embrace, for a moment he could forget the audit pressure, media slander, and political uncertainty. Here, in their private space, he just wanted to be Reza, Nisa's husband, drawing strength from his wife.
“They won't succeed in separating us, Mas,” Nisa whispered against Reza's chest. “Whatever they throw, we face it together.”
Reza tightened his embrace. “Always,” he answered.

Though the storm had just begun, the foundation of their relationship, tested by time and previous crises, still stood firm that night. However, they both knew, this was just the beginning. The real battle still stretched ahead, and their enemy seemed ready to use every means to destroy them.
6: Obor Nusa High School, South Jakarta, and a Mid-Class Cafe

Amid the bustling corridors of Obor Nusa High School filled with laughter, chatter, and the hurried footsteps of students from the country's most influential families, Vania Adiratna walked with a different aura. Not an arrogant or indifferent aura like some other students, but a calm, focused aura, her intelligent brown eyes always seeming to observe and analyze, holding great ambition behind a simple but neat appearance. Her uniform shirt was always crisply ironed, her skirt fit just below the knee, and her long black hair tied in a practical ponytail. Vania was an anomaly at this elite school. She got in not because of her parents' big name or family fortune, but purely through a full merit scholarship she'd won with great difficulty. Her background was far from her friends' glamour. Her mother was a nurse working double shifts, her father had long left them, and young Vania had to help bear the burden of caring for her sick grandmother while making sure her younger brother could still go to school properly. Their small rented house on the city outskirts was a world 180 degrees different from the European-style mansions or spacious villas with swimming pools owned by her schoolmates.

This gap, instead of making her feel inferior, actually became a whip for Vania. She studied harder than anyone, her grades never slipping from the top rank. The English debate club was her stage to show argumentative skill, and science olympiads were an arena to prove her intelligence. She was polite to teachers, kept a polite distance from friends too focused on lifestyle, and spent most of her time in the library or working part-time as a private tutor after school. Her goal was one: to win a full scholarship to a renowned university abroad, change her family's fate, prove she could shine despite coming from a difficult background.

It was this burning ambition, added to her intelligence and naturally attractive appearance, that made her 'seen.' Not by her peers, but by the sharp eyes of Auntie Widya. That middle-aged woman, introducing herself as a 'career mentor' and 'young talent scout,' approached Vania one afternoon at the public library, where Vania usually studied late.

With a motherly smile and words full of praise for Vania's achievements, Auntie Widya succeeded in winning the girl's trust in a short time. She listened to Vania's story about her family's difficulties with full sympathy, then, in their next meeting at a cafe slightly more upscale than what Vania usually visited, she offered a 'helping hand.'

“I see extraordinary potential in you, Vania,” Auntie Widya said while stirring her cappuccino. “It would be such a shame if that potential were hindered just because of cost issues. I have several contacts at international scholarship foundations and also at several big companies. I can help open a path for you.”
Vania's eyes sparkled, a bright glimmer of hope appearing in her heart often clouded by anxiety about the future. “Really, Auntie? I… I'm very grateful….”

Auntie Widya smiled soothingly. “Of course. I'm happy to help talented young people like you. But,” she paused briefly, looking at Vania with a 'wise' gaze, “in this life, building networks is very important, child. Academic ability alone is sometimes not enough. You have to be good at socializing, especially with people who can give you positive influence.”

She continued, her tone sounding light as if just sharing ordinary advice. “I hear you're at the same school as the president's son, Alex Satria? A very smart kid, but maybe a little… lonely? His parents must be very busy.” Vania nodded, not knowing where this conversation was heading.

“Well, what a coincidence,” Auntie Widya continued. “Several colleagues of mine who care about the younger generation's education asked me to pass along a message. They hope Alex can get good company at his school. A friend who's smart, polite, has a broad outlook, can be invited to discuss positive things, not just a partying friend. You,” Auntie Widya pointed at Vania with a wide smile, “are a very ideal type of friend for him.”

She leaned forward slightly. “Try to be closer friends with him, Vania. Invite him to study together, discuss current issues, other positive activities. Show him there's quality friendship out there. This won't only be good for Alex, but also a golden opportunity for you to be known by circles of important people. Who knows, your closeness with Alex could become an added value when you apply for scholarships later? Consider this a social investment for your future.”

That request was framed so beautifully. Helping a 'lonely' president's son while also opening a path to a dream scholarship. Vania, thirsty for opportunity and recognition, swallowed that bait whole. Small doubts about Auntie Widya's motive or the ethics of 'befriending with purpose' she pushed far away. This was her chance. She had to take it.

“Alright, Auntie,” Vania answered firmly, hiding the thumping in her chest. “I'll try.” She didn't yet realize she'd just agreed to become a pawn in a dangerous game designed by people like Hardiman Suryo, who saw Alex not as a lonely young person, but as the presidential family's weak point that could be exploited.

While Vania began planning her 'approach,' Alex Satria was in a vulnerable emotional state. The slander attacking his father's business these past weeks truly affected the atmosphere at home. His father, Reza, usually full of jokes and positive energy, now more often looked gloomy, tired, and easily irritated. His mother, Nisa, though trying to stay steady, clearly carried a heavy burden on her shoulders. Conversations among the three of them became rare and often ended in tension or awkward silence.

Alex felt like a stranger in his own home. He missed the warmth and attention of his parents, now drained by the political and business storm. He felt misunderstood, his complaints about school or friends felt trivial compared to the 'adult' problems his parents were facing. This emptiness made him crave a connection outside home, a connection with someone who could see him as Alex, not just as the president's son whose life was full of privilege, but complicated. His more intense meeting with Vania Adiratna at the library some time ago felt like an answer to that emptiness. Starting from an 'accidental' quantum physics discussion, their conversation flowed naturally into various topics. Alex found an intellectually matching conversation partner, something he rarely encountered. Vania wasn't just smart, but also a good listener. She seemed interested in Alex's thoughts, praised his ideas, and laughed at his corny jokes.

Alex couldn't deny his physical attraction to Vania. Her sweet smile, expressive eyes, and polite but confident attitude radiated their own charm. With Vania, Alex felt he could be himself. He could talk about the strangest scientific theory or complain about his math teacher without feeling judged or considered childish.

“You're the only person at this school who seems to get it when I bring up multiverses,” Alex said, laughing while they were on lunch break in the school garden, sitting a bit away from the crowded cafeteria.

Vania laughed along softly. “Maybe because we're both a little weird?” she replied playfully, her eyes twinkling. “But seriously, I like hearing your ideas. You have a different perspective, Lex.” That praise, though part of her 'strategy,' felt sincere as she said it. Her interaction with Alex began feeling like more than just a task.
Alex felt his cheeks warm slightly. He was happy being near Vania. This girl made him feel seen, heard, and valued. A feeling he'd missed so much lately.

The urge to spend more time with Vania grew stronger. He wanted to know this girl more beyond school scope. So that afternoon, as they walked together toward the school gate after debate club activity, Alex worked up the courage. “Vania,” he called a little nervously. “I heard there's a new documentary about Mars exploration at the theater this weekend. Would you… would you like to watch it with me? My treat.”

Vania stopped walking, looking at Alex with a briefly surprised expression. This invitation felt more personal than just studying together. Her heart pounded. This was big progress for her 'task.' Auntie Widya would surely be very pleased. But, another feeling emerged. A feeling of nervousness and a little… happiness?
She remembered Auntie Widya's message: 'social investment.' She also remembered her ambition. Then she looked into Alex's eyes, which looked full of hope.
“I'd love to, Lex!” Vania finally answered, trying to show the most natural enthusiastic smile she could. “I'm curious about that film too.”

A new step had been taken. Alex, driven by sincere attraction and his emotional need, opened the door to deeper friendship. Vania, driven by manipulated ambition and the seed of feeling beginning to grow without her fully realizing it, stepped through that door. Neither knew, the road ahead of them wasn't straight and bright, but winding and full of hidden traps ready to swallow them anytime. The pawn had been activated on the chessboard, and the mastermind smiled from afar.
7: Istana Negara and Cyberspace

That disaster arrived unannounced, striking right at Istana Negara's heart as Nisa Farha was intently leading a limited coordination meeting discussing acceleration strategy for social aid budget absorption in eastern regions. The meeting room, usually formal but productive, instantly turned into a silent field full of tension. The productive atmosphere, where relevant ministers presented data and Nisa gave direction with her characteristic focus and calm, was suddenly tainted by the constant vibration of Angel Marina's phone.

Angel's phone, set to vibrate mode beside her laptop, buzzed violently as if possessed. Not one or two notifications, but a nonstop stream from various apps — the exploding internal communications team WhatsApp group, red-flagged urgent emails from the Palace cyber team, Google Alerts for the president's name, and notifications from dozens of online news apps. The preview headlines flashing briefly on the lock screen were enough to make Angel's blood feel frozen and her heart pound wildly.

With trembling hands, she tried opening one message from the Palace's social media team head. Its content was brief and panicked: “Mbak Angel, emergency! There's a video and photos resembling Madam President circulating widely! Very vulgar. Spreading so fast!” Accompanied by a link from an obscure news portal, SuaraRakyatNet.

Angel swallowed, working up courage to open that link. Her eyes widened in horror. Her tablet screen now displayed a collage of high-quality images, capturing a woman extraordinarily resembling Nisa Farha — her haircut, face shape, even the small mole near her lip — in various intimate and explicit poses with a man. The image quality was quite good, the lighting looked natural, making it appear very authentic at first glance. Worse, there were links to several short video clips lasting a few seconds, uploaded on hard-to-trace anonymous platforms, showing similar scenes with manipulated soft moaning sounds. The man in that visual material was quickly 'confirmed' by anonymous gossip accounts as Zidan Hidayat — Nisa's ex-boyfriend from college, an architect now publicly known to have divorced.

The headlines framing that material were so sensational, merciless: “THE BIGGEST SCANDAL OF THE CENTURY? Hot Video Resembling President Nisa and Ex-Boyfriend Shakes Cyberspace!”, “Morality Questioned: Nisa Farha's Wild Past Trail Uncovered?”, “#NisaZidanTrending, People Deeply Disappointed!”

This wasn't just news. This was a planned, brutal attack, designed to totally destroy Nisa. Angel looked at Nisa, who still hadn't realized the tsunami that had just struck her reputation. She exchanged a panicked glance with Anton Prasetya across the table, whose face was also already deathly pale, clearly having received similar news.

Nisa felt the drastic change in that room. The budget discussion stopped. The ministers who'd been focused now whispered to each other, their faces tense, some even openly checking their phones with shocked expressions. Awkward silence blanketed the room. “What's going on?” Nisa finally asked, her voice still calm, but a curious tone and bad premonition beginning to sound clear. “Why does everyone look anxious?”

Anton Prasetya, after taking a long breath and exchanging a brief glance with Angel, worked up courage to step forward. He couldn't manage words, only handing his tablet displaying one of the most vulgar news items to Nisa.

Nisa took that tablet, her brow furrowing. She read the headline, then her eyes fixed on the photos below. Instantly, Nisa's world seemed to stop spinning, went hollow, then collapsed into pieces. Her breath caught as if an invisible hand was strangling her neck. Her face, which had radiated leadership aura, instantly turned pale, blood seeming to drain from it. That tablet shook violently in her trembling hand. Those images… that video… That wasn't her! That was slander! But the resemblance… the detail… so precise, so terrifying. And Zidan… why Zidan? A past she'd buried deep, a college puppy-love story long over… why was it now resurrected in the cruelest way?

“No, this… this isn't true…,” Nisa whispered weakly, more to herself. Her head felt light, dizzy, the room seemed to spin. Nausea rose to her throat. A deep sense of humiliation, the feeling of having her privacy brutally violated, burning anger, and paralyzing fear — all mixed into one storm of emotion striking her consciousness.

The meeting dispersed in silent chaos. The ministers excused themselves one by one with concerned faces, but also full of question marks, leaving Nisa slumped, supported by Angel and Anton back to her private office.

That news spread faster than lightning. Within an hour, Indonesia was in uproar. The hashtag #SkandalPresidenNisa became the world's number one trending topic. Family WhatsApp groups, social gathering groups, to school alumni groups buzzed discussing it. Social media timelines split into two camps fiercely attacking each other.

Nisa's supporters moved militantly. They created counter-hashtags #SayaPercayaPresidenNisa, #LawanHoaxDeepfake. They shared simple technical analysis about the possibility of AI manipulation, comparing details of Nisa's real photos with the fake ones. They reminded the public of Nisa's achievements, of the Family Readiness Bill she'd just fought for. Women activists spoke loudly against the sexist and misogynistic attack targeting Nisa.

However, that defensive voice felt like a small boat amid a storm of condemnation. The majority of the shocked public, or those already antipathetic toward Nisa, easily swallowed whole that so 'convincing' visual material. Comments full of insults, disappointment, and judgment flooded comment columns wherever that news appeared. Sarcastic memes and parody videos emerged. Nisa's image as a moral role model instantly collapsed.

Reza Satria, who'd just felt a little relief after successfully parrying the slander attack on his business, felt his world turned upside down again as he landed at Halim Perdanakusuma. His phone notifications exploded. As soon as he saw the images and video of his wife, anger bigger than before burned within him. This was no longer about business or politics. This was about the honor of the woman he loved most.

He arrived at the Palace like a wounded bull, barging into Nisa's office. Seeing Nisa's fragile condition, sitting frozen with a blank stare, Reza's anger subsided a little, replaced by pain and an extraordinary urge to protect.
“Nisa!” he called weakly, kneeling, cupping his wife's face. “Look at me! This is slander! Fabrication! You believe that, right? We'll fight this together!”

Nisa looked into Reza's eyes. She saw anger there, but also sincere worry. She nodded weakly. “I know, Mas. But… it feels like being stripped naked in front of the whole world,” she whispered hoarsely, tears finally flowing.

Reza embraced her tightly. “I know, love. I know how much it hurts. But you're not alone. I'm here.” He felt Nisa's body trembling in his embrace. “Whoever did this… they won't get away with it. I swear.” Behind his oath, fear flickered. What kind of enemy could do something this vile? How big was their power?

The political impact rolled fast. The Palace was flooded with calls from party leaders, community figures, to friendly countries' ambassadors requesting clarification. Hardiman Suryo quickly appeared like a self-appointed hero, holding a press conference, voicing 'deep concern' over 'moral decadence' tarnishing state dignity, and implicitly questioning Nisa's fitness to lead.

Coalition parties panicked. Nisa's electability, which had been skyrocketing, was now threatened with free-fall. The election drew closer. Party leaders began recalculating their political math. Calls from the chairman of Nisa's sponsoring party, usually warm, now felt cold and full of small talk. Pressure on Nisa to withdraw or at least 'rest' for the sake of 'saving the party' began being heard faintly. The presidential candidate registration deadline felt increasingly strangling.

In her office, now feeling cold and foreign, Nisa felt isolated in a storm created by her enemies. This attack was different. Crueler, more personal, more destructive. She looked at Reza, still faithfully by her side, but she knew her husband's burden was also already so heavy. Her logic and calm as a leader seemed to evaporate, replaced by fear, anger, and creeping panic. Who? How? Why? Those questions spun without answer, drowning her in an ocean of despair. The Palace, which should be the center of her strength, now felt like the epicenter of her destruction.
8: A Few Days After the Scandal Exploded
Istana Negara and Obor Nusa High School Surroundings

Several days had passed since the 'bomb' of the fake Nisa-Zidan video scandal exploded, but its shock still felt strong throughout Istana Negara, especially within the presidential couple's private pavilion's silence. The air felt heavy, laden with unspoken tension. Nisa Farha and Reza Satria moved around each other like two planets out of their orbit — still bound to each other by the invisible gravity called love and fifteen years of commitment, but their trajectories no longer synced, disturbed by the external storm forcing them to spin in their own respective anxieties.

Nisa spent most of her time in her office, burying herself in piles of state documents or virtual meetings with her team. This was her way of surviving: working, maintaining routine, rebuilding the wall of professionalism that had crumbled from that personal attack. But at night, when it was just her and Reza, that wall felt so thin. She missed her husband's warm embrace, their light conversation, but she didn't know how to start. Every time she tried opening a conversation about her feelings — humiliation, fear, anger — she saw a flash of such deep exhaustion in Reza's eyes, and those words got stuck in her throat. She didn't want to add to Reza's burden, clearly already very heavy.

Reza, on the other hand, was also trapped in his own struggle. His anger at his wife's slanderers still burned, but now mixed with frustration and exhaustion from the double attack — on his business and now on Nisa's honor. He spent his energy coordinating with the legal team, the Palace's communications team, and even Reza Satria Group's internal security team to trace the slander's source and prepare rebuttals. He wanted to protect Nisa, to be a shield for his wife, but he felt he'd failed. That attack was too brutal, too fast. And seeing Nisa now more often silent, withdrawing behind her mask of composure, made Reza feel increasingly distant and helpless. He wanted to reach for Nisa, but he was afraid of saying the wrong thing, afraid of adding to his wife's wound.
Their dinners became a painful silent ritual. Sitting facing each other at a dining table that felt too big, they mostly stared at their own plates rather than exchanging glances.
“How was your meeting with the legal team earlier, Mas?” Nisa asked one night, trying to break the silence.

“Slow,” Reza answered briefly, sounding tired. “They're still trying to analyze that video's metadata. Very hard to trace its original source.” He paused, then asked back, “Have you… taken your medicine?” A standard question now feeling like a formality replacing their intimacy.

“Yes,” Nisa answered quietly. The conversation stopped there. Both sank back into their own thoughts, separated by an invisible chasm created by the storm outside. The warmth and openness that once characterized their relationship was now covered by a thick fog of misunderstanding and uncommunicated stress. That initial crack began showing clearly on the surface of their always-seemingly-perfect marriage.

Meanwhile, far from the Palace's tension, Alex Satria actually found his 'escape.' The gloomy home atmosphere and his parents looking so fragile and distant made him feel increasingly alienated and useless. He needed fresh air, needed distraction, needed someone who could make him feel normal even for a moment. And Vania Adiratna cleverly filled that void.

The invitation to watch the Mars documentary last weekend went 'successfully' — at least from Vania's viewpoint, who reported 'significant progress' to Auntie Widya. For Alex, watching the film with Vania was indeed enjoyable. They could excitedly discuss the possibility of life on other planets after the film ended. Vania again showed her intelligence matching Alex's, but also her humorous side that made Alex laugh — something he'd rarely done these past few weeks.

However, behind that momentary joy, unease within Alex actually kept growing. His closeness with Vania felt increasingly intense, and somehow, increasingly suffocating. Vania was now almost always present at every opportunity. Sending good-morning messages every day, asking about Alex's schedule, 'coincidentally' appearing at the cafeteria while Alex was eating, or waiting for him in front of class at dismissal time.

Vania's attention felt so total, but sometimes excessive. She often praised Alex specifically, not just his intelligence, but also his appearance, his way of talking, as if Alex were the center of her world. At first Alex felt flattered, but gradually that praise felt a little… empty? Or maybe too arranged?

Vania also began often 'confiding' to Alex. About how heavy her family's burden was, how she felt alone and needed a true friend, how Alex was the only person who truly 'understood' her. This confiding made Alex feel sorry as well as responsible for Vania's happiness. It was hard for him to refuse Vania's invitations or keep distance when Vania showed her fragile side like that.

“I'm so happy I can be close to you like this, Lex,” Vania said one afternoon as they sat at the edge of the school basketball court, waiting for the rain to stop. “It feels like… you're the first person who really sees me as I am, not just as 'the smart one' or 'the scholarship kid'.” She looked at Alex with hopeful, glistening eyes.

Alex felt torn. On one hand, he was happy to be an 'important person' to Vania. But on the other, he felt the increasingly large pressure of expectation from that girl. He wasn't ready for a more serious relationship, especially amid the storm hitting his family. But how to say it to Vania without hurting that girl's feelings, who seemed so sincere (and fragile)?
“I'm happy being friends with you too, Vania,” Alex answered carefully, choosing the word 'friends'.

Vania's expression changed slightly disappointed hearing the word 'friends,' but only briefly. She quickly smiled again. “Yeah, friends…, close friends,” she corrected, as if asserting the level of their relationship as she wished. “Close friends have to support each other, right? So, if you have a problem, just tell me, okay? Don't keep it bottled up. Especially about… well, you know… the news about your mother.” Vania tried to probe with a tone full of sympathy.

Alex instantly felt uncomfortable. He wasn't ready to discuss his mother's problem with anyone, let alone Vania. “I… I'm fine,” Alex deflected quickly. “My mom is strong, she'll surely get through this.” “Of course,” Vania replied quickly, realizing she might have gone too far. “But if you need anything at all, I'm ready to help, you know.” She patted the back of Alex's hand gently.

That touch again. It felt warm, but somehow also felt like a subtle snare increasingly binding Alex. He began feeling guilty for not being able to fully reciprocate Vania's 'sincerity.' He began questioning his own feelings. Was he too cold? Was he insensitive? That gaslighting worked slowly, but effectively.

Alex didn't know that behind that sweet and fragile attitude, Vania was carrying out a mission directed by Auntie Widya. He also didn't know that Vania herself was beginning to feel internal turmoil; guilt from manipulating Alex mixed with sincere attraction growing beyond her control, making her increasingly reckless in 'trapping' Alex.

The initial crack wasn't only happening in Nisa and Reza's marriage battered by an external storm. In Alex's teenage world, another crack began forming from within, triggered by external manipulation and internal fragility. A relationship that should have been an escape for Alex actually had the potential to become a new trap no less dangerous. Unease began hanging thick, both within the Palace walls and in that elite school's corridors.
9: A Few Days Later
Istana Negara, Jakarta

Istana Negara's grand, sturdy walls now felt like they were closing in, pressing on Nisa Farha from all directions. The air inside the air-conditioned presidential compound felt stifling, laden with unheard whispers, question-mark-filled stares, and increasingly brutal political pressure by the day. Every phone ring, every news notification, every report from the communications team felt like a new needle piercing her already too-thin skin.

Nisa felt she was at her breaking point. Her sleep was only fragments of restless nightmares. Her appetite was gone. State meetings she once led with focus and energy now felt like a heavy burden she had to drag with the last of her strength. She saw her reflection in the mirror — pale, tired, with thick dark circles under her eyes that even the best makeup couldn't disguise. This was no longer the face of the inspiring President Nisa Farha; this was the face of a woman being slowly destroyed.

The slander attack on Reza still loomed, disturbing her husband's concentration and creating distance between them. The fake video scandal of herself and Zidan kept being fodder for gossip media and a weapon for political opponents. And worst of all, she felt isolated exactly when she most needed support.

Reza… her husband was indeed still there. Physically, he accompanied Nisa, held her hand, spoke words of support. But Nisa could feel the heavy burden Reza also carried — stress from his disturbed business, anger over the slander hitting his wife, and perhaps, deep in his heart, a glimmer of unspoken doubt though Reza tried to deny it. Reza was mostly silent, sunk in his own work or meetings with the legal team. Nisa could no longer share her fragility, afraid it would only add to the burden on Reza's shoulders, which already felt about to break.

Angel and Anton, her two trusted staff, worked tirelessly on the front line, trying to extinguish the gossip fire, preparing rebuttals, and protecting the Palace's image. But Nisa saw the concerned look in their eyes, a look that felt like a mix of loyalty and pity. She didn't want to be pitied. She was President of the Republic of Indonesia, not a patient needing care. This feeling made her keep more distance, limiting interaction only to the most urgent work matters.

What about Dinda? Her best friend? Nisa had thought of calling Dinda, pouring out all her panic, seeking a friendship's embrace that might calm her. Dinda would surely listen with full sympathy, giving unconditional support as usual. But… Nisa hesitated. This wasn't just an ordinary political matter. This concerned Zidan, her past. Something that felt too personal, too complicated to share, even with her closest friend. Besides, Nisa felt she needed a quick solution, not just venting. She felt she had to act alone before it was too late. Involving Dinda would only slow things down or perhaps add complication. No, she had to resolve this herself first.
Amid this solitude and desperation, Nisa's mind became increasingly obsessed with one name: Zidan Hidayat.

Zidan was the key. She had to talk to Zidan. Why was Zidan's face used in that fabricated video? Did Zidan know something? Was he forced? Could he help Nisa prove that video was fake? Nisa felt only Zidan could give a definite answer, an answer she could use to fight back, to clear her name before everything was truly too late.

The Palace team might be working to trace the video's source, but that would take time. Parties were already starting to waver, the nomination deadline drew closer. Nisa felt she didn't have much time. Meeting Zidan directly felt like the only shortcut, the only hope remaining.

But how? Order BIN or the Police to find and bring Zidan to the Palace? Too risky to leak and would trigger new speculation. Ask Angel or Anton to arrange a secret meeting? Nisa felt unsure they could do it undetected by the enemy network that seemed so wide and strong.
The more Nisa thought about it in her sleepless nights, the more convinced she became: she had to go alone. Quietly. Without involving anyone.

That decision was crazy. Reckless. Contrary to all common sense and a head of state's security protocol. Nisa knew that. But panic is a wild beast that can devour logic. In her pressured condition, Nisa convinced herself this was the only way. She had to take this risk to save her honor, her family, and perhaps also the future of her leadership. This was no longer the act of a president, but the act of a cornered and desperate Nisa Farha.

A plan began forming in her troubled mind. She would use the weekend, when her schedule was a bit looser and security might not be as tight as on weekdays. She'd use the excuse of needing alone time to walk in the Palace's back garden. Then, at a camera blind spot she knew, she'd slip out through a rarely used side door.

She'd prepared a makeshift disguise: a wide headscarf, big sunglasses, a medical mask. She'd also reactivated her old prepaid SIM card and prepared some cash. She'd found the address of Zidan's firm office in Kemang through an online search she did quietly on her personal laptop. She hoped to meet Zidan there, or at least get information on his home address.

The risk? Extraordinarily large. Being caught by presidential guards before successfully getting out. Being recognized by people on the street. A suspicious taxi driver. Zidan refusing to meet or even reacting negatively. Or the worst possibility: being followed by her enemies who might have anticipated her move. But Nisa pushed aside all that fear. Panic gave her false courage. She felt she had to do this. There was no other choice.

The night before the planned D-day (Saturday morning), Nisa could barely sleep at all. Her heart pounded fast. She rechecked her small bag containing the disguise, old phone, and cash. She looked at herself in the mirror, trying to convince herself she could do this. The face in that mirror looked foreign — pale, tense, with a wild look in her eyes.

She glanced at the other side of the bed where Reza slept (or perhaps just pretended to sleep), his back facing Nisa. There was a great urge to wake Reza, tell him her plan, ask for support or even prohibition. But Nisa held back. She didn't want to add to Reza's burden. She didn't want to see disappointment or fear in her husband's eyes. This was her own battle.

With a heavy heart, Nisa steadied her resolve. Tomorrow morning, she would step out of her golden cage, toward dangerous uncertainty, armed only with a fragile hope of finding an answer from a man from her past. A panicked decision that would change the course of her life forever, in a way she never imagined.
10: Saturday Morning
South Jakarta

Jakarta's sky that Saturday morning stayed faithful to its gray overcast, as if becoming a fitting backdrop for the reckless mission Nisa Farha was undertaking. Armed with the excuse of wanting to find solitude alone, Nisa succeeded in fooling her aide and presidential guard. With her heart pounding hard behind her wide headscarf and sunglasses disguise, she walked calmly in the Palace's back garden, then at the camera blind spot she'd memorized, she quickly slipped through a small side door in the Palace wall.

Success! She was outside. Adrenaline pumped her blood faster, overcoming her momentary fear. She walked quickly through a quiet alley toward the main road, managing to hail a conventional taxi without being recognized by its half-drowsy driver. She named a shopping center near Kemang as her initial destination.

The journey felt torturous. Every red light, every small traffic jam, felt like adding to Nisa's anxiety burden. Her mind kept spinning: What would she say to Zidan? What if Zidan got angry? What if Zidan refused to talk? What if… if Zidan was involved in that video? That last possibility felt the most painful.

After getting off not far from her destination mall, Nisa walked toward Zidan's firm's office address. Quiet. That office was closed on Saturday. Disappointment and panic began creeping through Nisa. But she remembered Zidan's old story about his small studio apartment near the office. Arkanasya Residence.
With last hope, Nisa walked again toward that mid-class apartment. In the lobby, she managed to fool the receptionist by saying she already had an appointment, and got Zidan's unit number: 1208.

The elevator felt to move so slowly carrying her to the 12th floor. A quiet corridor greeted her. She stood before unit 1208's wooden door, taking a deep breath, trying to calm her wildly racing heartbeat. She knocked. Once. Twice.
Silence.

A bad premonition began creeping over her. She tried the door handle. Unlocked. Slightly ajar. Odd. Zidan cared very much about privacy and security. “Zidan?” Nisa called softly, pushing the door slightly wider open. “It's me, Nisa.”
Silence.
Only the soft hum of the air conditioner. And… a strange smell. A faint but piercing metallic bloody smell, making Nisa's stomach instantly nauseous.
With trembling steps, Nisa entered. That studio apartment's condition was in disarray. Drawing papers scattered, a chair overturned. The bloody smell grew stronger. Her eyes swept the room in panic.

Then she saw it. In the corner near the curtained balcony window, a man's body lay face down. A t-shirt, shorts. An unnatural position. And a pool of dark liquid — blood — around his head, partly beginning to dry at its edges, but its middle still looked wet.
Nisa froze. That was Zidan! She recognized that body posture.

“Zidan…?” she whispered hoarsely. Her legs weakened, unable to step closer. The smell of death felt so thick. An unnatural death. And seeing the blood's condition, this seemed to have just happened yesterday. Not long ago.

Nisa's head spun violently. The room seemed to spin. She stepped back, hand covering her mouth holding back a scream. This wasn't just a clarification meeting. This was… murder! Who could be so cruel to do this? And why?

Nisa's thought immediately jumped to one conclusion: A trap! This must be a trap! Someone killed Zidan then deliberately left this door open so she'd find him! So she'd be accused! Her instinct screamed telling her to run. Get away from here as fast as possible!

Just as she was about to turn around, the sound of a key being inserted into the door lock from outside was heard so clearly in that apartment's silence. Followed by the sound of the door opening wider. Nisa's heart seemed to stop beating. Who was that? The killer? Police?

The first figure to appear was Reza. His face was pale, full of worry he couldn't hide. Behind him, Angel Marina, with a similar expression. And lastly… Dinda Larasati, her friend, with a pale face and reddened eyes as if having just cried from anxiety.

The three of them froze at the doorway. Their eyes widened in extraordinary shock seeing Nisa standing trembling in the middle of the room. Then their gaze shifted to the room's corner, to Zidan's figure lying horrifically.

“NISA?!” Reza exclaimed in disbelief, his voice a mix of momentary relief finding his wife and horrified shock seeing the scene before him. “W-what are you doing here?! And… Oh God…, is that… Zidan?!”

Angel gasped, covering her mouth with both hands, tears immediately flowing heavily seeing the horror before her and Nisa's clearly shaken condition. Dinda screamed softly, her body swaying and she leaned against the doorframe, her eyes widening in horror staring at the corpse then alternating toward Nisa with an expression of disbelief and full of sympathy. The three of their reactions — Reza, Angel, and Dinda — looked exactly the same: shock, horror, and extraordinary confusion.
For Nisa, panicking and paranoid, their presence at this moment, with the same shocked expression, felt like confirmation that she'd walked into a trap. This situation was perfect to entrap her.

But for Nisa, struck by paranoia and shock, the arrival of the three of them — Reza, Angel, and especially Dinda, her friend — at this most crucial moment felt like the worst nightmare. They found her here! At Zidan's murder scene! Right after she entered! This couldn't possibly be coincidence! “This… this isn't what it looks like!” Nisa exclaimed in panic, her voice trembling violently. “I swear! I just arrived! The door wasn't locked! I don't know anything! This is a trap!”

But her words sounded desperate. She saw the shocked, confused, horrified expression on Reza's and Angel's faces. And Dinda… her friend looked so shaken, so sad seeing Nisa in this situation, her tears flowing heavily. Everyone's reaction was so real, so spontaneous. But that was exactly what made Nisa panic even more. If they didn't trap her, then who? And why could they arrive here this fast?
Nisa felt cornered. Trapped. Whoever the mastermind was, they'd succeeded in making her look guilty. The instinct to flee took over her entire consciousness.

Before Reza, Angel, or Dinda could fully process the situation or approach her, Nisa acted impulsively. She spun her body, running with all her strength toward the balcony door on the other side of the room that was slightly open. She forced it open.
“NISA! DON'T!” Reza shouted in panic, trying to step forward.

But Nisa had already jumped out onto the narrow 12th-floor balcony, climbing its railing nimbly like a possessed person, then jumping onto the canopy roof of the floor below. A dangerous acrobatic act born of total desperation.
From the canopy roof, she jumped again onto the empty balcony of the neighboring unit, then disappeared inside before anyone could react further.

Reza, Angel, and Dinda could only stand frozen in Zidan's apartment, now feeling increasingly cold and gripping. They stared in horror toward the balcony where Nisa had just disappeared like a shadow, then looked back at Zidan's stiff corpse. Shock. Confusion. Fear. What had just happened? Why was Nisa here? Why was Zidan killed? And most terrifying, why did Nisa flee like that? Those questions hung in the air, unanswered, creating a new chapter far darker and more dangerous for all of them.
11: The Same Day and Following Days
Zidan's Apartment, Istana Negara and Nisa's Hiding Place

The trip back to Istana Negara felt like crossing another dimension. Reza Satria, Angel Marina, and Dinda Larasati sat silently in the fast-moving presidential car, each sunk in the horror and confusion over what they'd just witnessed. Zidan Hidayat's corpse. And Nisa Farha, President of the Republic of Indonesia, was there, then fled like a shadow.

“We… we can't tell anyone Nisa was there earlier,” Reza's voice broke the silence first, hoarse and full of pressure. He looked at Angel through the rearview mirror. “You know what will happen if this leaks, right?”
Angel nodded stiffly, her face still deathly pale. “Ruined, Pak Reza. Everything will be destroyed. Madam President will immediately be accused…” She couldn't continue.

“Oh God, Nisa…” Dinda sobbed from the back seat, her shoulders shaking. “She must be so scared! She must feel trapped! What should we do, Mas Reza? We have to help Nisa!” Her voice sounded so sincere, full of a true friend's panic and worry.

Reza took a long breath, trying to control the turmoil in his chest. Worry for Nisa's safety mixed with confusion over his wife's act of fleeing. But one thing was certain, he had to protect Nisa. “We'll help Nisa, Dinda,” he said, trying to sound calm. “But first, we have to control this situation. We mustn't panic.”

Arriving at the Palace, Reza immediately moved fast. He contacted Anton Prasetya through a secure channel, informing him of Zidan's body discovery (without mentioning Nisa), asking Anton to secretly contact the Police Chief for very confidential and sensitive crime scene handling. He also asked Anton to deploy the internal security team to quietly begin searching for Nisa, assuming Nisa might just be hiding somewhere from severe shock.

The next step was to meet Vice President Pradipta Angkasa. An emergency meeting was held that night at the Situation Room. Only the five of them: VP Pradipta suddenly summoned, Reza, Angel, Anton, and Dinda (whom Reza asked to join as Nisa's friend who best knew Nisa's recent condition).

With a heavy voice holding back emotion, Reza explained the real situation to VP Pradipta. About Nisa recklessly meeting Zidan because of the video scandal's pressure, about Zidan's body discovery, about Nisa's presence at the scene, and about Nisa's flight clearly driven by panic and a feeling of being trapped. Reza fought desperately to convince the VP that Nisa couldn't possibly be involved in that murder.

VP Pradipta listened with a deeply furrowed brow, his face serious weighing the extraordinarily complex constitutional and political implications. Angel and Anton added details about Nisa's mental condition, indeed very stressed these past days. Dinda added, her voice choked with tears, “That's right, Mr. Vice President. Nisa, my friend, has been very fragile lately. She must have been in severe shock to act beyond control. We have to protect her.” After a gripping silence, VP Pradipta made a heavy decision. “State stability is the top priority,” he said firmly. “We can't let news of the President being at a murder scene and fleeing spread widely. We have to cover this up, at least temporarily, while we search for Madam President and uncover the truth of Zidan's case.”

He continued, “Official story: President Nisa Farha is experiencing acute physical and mental exhaustion. The presidential medical team recommends total rest and intensive care at a private location for recovery. I will carry out presidential duties temporarily according to the constitution.” He looked sharply at the Palace team. “Angel, Anton, prepare a press release, coordinate all lines. Make sure this narrative is consistent.” Then to Reza and Dinda, “I hope you two can help maintain this story.”
Reza and Dinda nodded in agreement, both looking equally relieved that Nisa wouldn't be immediately 'judged' by the public.

The announcement of President Nisa's 'illness' shocked Indonesia the next day. Media questioned, the public speculated. What illness? Why so sudden? Was it related to the Zidan case? The Palace answered all questions with a standard statement about the president's need for privacy during recovery. Hardiman Suryo used this moment to question Nisa's capacity to lead and demanded transparency, but he didn't know Nisa truly wasn't at the Palace.

In a cramped rented house in Senen, Nisa learned of her 'illness news' from a beat-up television. She was stunned. So they chose to lie? To protect her? Or to confine her? The relief of not being hunted by the public mixed with growing paranoia. Why would they lie if they believed she was innocent? Did they have another agenda? Distrust of her inner circle thickened, though she couldn't point to who should be suspected. Reza? Angel? Or even Dinda, her friend? That thought made her feel increasingly alone and isolated. She had to find evidence herself, right now, before this lie collapsed.

The following days at the Palace ran full of pretense and pressure. Reza split his focus between audited business meetings, accompanying Alex at the hospital (who now also wondered why his mother couldn't visit him), coordinating with the team searching for Nisa (which yielded nothing), and playing his role as the 'steady husband' before VP Pradipta and the public.

Angel and Anton struggled to counter wild issues in media, answer reporters' questions, and keep government operations running smoothly under VP Pradipta. They also quietly tried gathering initial information about Zidan's case, feeling there were many oddities, but had no strong lead yet.

Amid all that, Dinda Larasati was present as an extraordinary oasis. She came almost every day, bringing food for Reza or the Palace team, visiting Alex with a sympathetic face, even offering to help Angel sort support letters for Nisa.

“Mas Reza should eat a lot, so you stay strong,” she said one afternoon while placing a tiffin container with Reza's favorite oxtail soup on Reza's desk at the Palace (Reza often worked there to stay close to the information center). “I know this is really heavy for Mas Reza.” Her hand patted Reza's shoulder gently, her gaze full of understanding.

“Thank you so much, Dinda,” Reza answered sincerely, feeling touched by his wife's friend's consistent attention. “You're truly a real friend to Nisa, and to all of us.” He was the one who felt guilty whenever he sometimes felt a little bothered by Dinda's too-frequent presence — that must be because he himself was under severe stress.

A fragile public lie, maintained by a handful of people struck by stress and uncertainty, while the president herself struggled alone in hiding. The secret of the missing president was kept tight, but became a time bomb. Political and media pressure kept rising.

The storm might have subsided a little on the surface of public opinion, but behind it, the undercurrent of intrigue and danger actually grew stronger and more unpredictable. The Satria family was pierced, wounded, and imprisoned from various sides. Let's keep praying and hoping that President Nisa can soon be found.
12: Today, Second Week Since Nisa's 'Illness'
Istana Negara, Jakarta VVIP Hospital, Mass Media

The air at Istana Negara felt increasingly thin each day. Not from lack of oxygen, but from the thick layer of pressure, secrecy, and anxiety enveloping every corridor corner, every meeting room, even every breath of its occupants. Entering the second week since President Nisa Farha's official 'illness' announcement, the Palace felt like an aircraft carrier leaking at four hull points at once, while the storm outside showed no sign of subsiding. The remaining core team — Reza Satria, Angel Marina, Anton Prasetya, under VP Pradipta Angkasa's temporary command — ran from one fire point to another, trying to extinguish the blaze while keeping their biggest secret from burning up too.
Those four battle fronts now felt like a four-headed monster continuously gnawing at them:

One: The Ghost of the Nisa-Zidan Video Scandal. Though Alex's tragedy news now dominated more, that video scandal's ghost refused to die. Every few days, anonymous accounts or opposition news portals would again 'remind' the public about it, re-uploading image or video fragments with new narratives questioning the 'ill' President's morality. The Palace cyber team was still stuck. That deepfake technology was too sophisticated, or maybe its spreader's source was too clever at erasing tracks. Doubt over Nisa's character remained a latent weapon ready to be detonated anytime.

Two: Alex Satria's Legal Storm. This was the most painful gaping wound for Reza, and became the most intense focus of public attention. The discovery of Vania Adiratna's pregnancy fact had changed everything. Media painted Alex as an irresponsible rich teenager who impregnated his girlfriend then killed her in panic. Vicious comments flooded news columns: “President's son, depraved behavior!”, “Life imprisonment!”, “The apple doesn't fall far from the tree?” — that last sentence implicitly linking it to Nisa's video scandal. Alex himself, in his sterile hospital room that felt like a prison, withdrew more. Physical and psychological trauma made it hard for him to give consistent statements to investigators, which actually further strengthened suspicion against him. The best lawyer team Reza hired worked day and night, but they fought against already-formed public opinion and a 'motive' that looked so clear on the surface.

Three: The Reza Satria Group Business Shock. The independent audit forced by political pressure ran arduously and exhaustingly. Every transaction, every contract, every past Reza business meeting was now ransacked, looking for the smallest gap. Though Reza was confident there was no legal violation, this process greatly disturbed his company's image and operations. Stock price corrected somewhat, several investors postponed investment decisions, and business partners began asking with a worried tone. Reza had to split his already-drained energy to lead his company through this turbulence, while continuing to deny baseless conflict-of-interest accusations.

Four: The Mystery of President Nisa's 'Illness.' This was a constitutional time bomb. The longer Nisa was 'absent' without transparent medical clarity, the bigger the pressure on VP Pradipta Angkasa. Public questioning shifted from sympathy to skepticism, then to demand. “What illness exactly?” “When can she return to duty?” “Is the state held hostage by the President's health condition?” Hardiman Suryo became the main orator voicing this doubt, appearing on various talk shows, pushing for an independent medical team to examine Nisa, a proposal clearly aimed at exposing the Palace's lie or forcing Nisa to resign due to 'permanent incapacity.' And behind the scenes, political lobbying grew more intense. Coalition parties, anxious about their electability in the upcoming election if continuously associated with a 'problematic' and 'sickly' President, began seriously considering 're-evaluating' their support for Nisa's second term. The presidential candidate registration deadline, less than two months away, felt like a Sword of Damocles hanging over the Palace team's heads.

Amid this whirlwind, the daily coordination meeting at the Situation Room became an arena for stress release as well as increasingly difficult crucial decision-making. VP Pradipta's face looked increasingly furrowed, though he tried to maintain his dignity. Angel and Anton looked sleep-deprived, their eyes reddened from staring at data screens too long and countering media attacks. Reza Satria… he looked like a shadow of his former self. Thinner, his gaze often blank, though he tried hard to stay focused and give strategic input.

“Progress on searching for Madam President… still nothing, Mr. Vice President, Pak Reza,” Anton reported quietly, as if not wanting to add burden to that room. “The team has combed all possible locations based on the latest data, but it's as if she vanished into thin air. Her old phone is also completely inactive.”

Reza closed his eyes hearing that report. The strangling worry struck him again. Where was Nisa? Was she safe? Was she eating? Was she cold? Or… had something bad happened to her? Those thoughts tormented him every second.
“We have to keep trying, Anton,” VP Pradipta said firmly. “Deploy all intelligence resources we can use secretly. We have to find Madam President before other parties find her.”

“Meanwhile, pressure from factions about the nomination is getting stronger,” Angel added. “The Pelopor Party Chairman even asked for a one-on-one meeting with Pak Wapres this week. Most likely to explore other options.”
VP Pradipta sighed. “Just arrange the meeting, Angel. We'll listen to their aspirations, but we won't make any decision yet now.”

Reza could only stay silent listening. It felt ironic. Once he and Nisa were so solid fighting for their shared vision. Now, Nisa had disappeared, he had to fight alone saving their son and family reputation, while the party that should support them actually began looking for a way to leave them. Politics was indeed cruel.
Amid that heavy meeting, the door was knocked again. Dinda Larasati appeared with her soothing gentle smile. Today she brought a big thermos of warm mung bean porridge and several small plates.

“Sorry to disturb again,” she said cheerfully, trying to lighten the mood. “I thought you all needed something warm and sweet to lift your spirits. This is Nisa's favorite mung bean porridge, a recipe straight from her mother, you know.” She began pouring porridge into small plates and distributing them.

“Oh my, Dinda, you never stop,” Angel said with a sincere smile, accepting a plate of porridge. “Thank you so much, so thoughtful.” “Yes, Dinda. Thank you,” Anton added. Dinda's always cheerful and supportive presence indeed felt like a little light amid the darkness enveloping them.

Dinda then approached Reza, placing a bowl of porridge before him. “Eat up, Mas Reza. Don't let your stomach stay empty. You have to take care of your health, you know,” she said with a tone full of sincere concern. Her hand patted Reza's shoulder again, longer than just an ordinary greeting. “I know Mas Reza must have the heaviest burden right now. But Mas Reza isn't alone. There's me, there's Angel, Anton, Mr. Vice President… we all support Mas Reza.”

Reza looked into Dinda's eyes, so sincerely sympathetic. He felt very grateful for his wife's friend's consistent support. Dinda smiled then sat briefly accompanying them, listening to Angel's complaints about buzzer attacks or Anton's story about arduous political lobbying, occasionally chiming in with encouraging words. She'd now become an inseparable part of the Palace's crisis circle.

Meanwhile, in her hiding place, Nisa stared at her old phone screen, reading news about VP Pradipta increasingly pressured by parties. She also read news about Alex's condition not significantly improving and how public opinion increasingly cornered him. The feeling of helplessness and urgency to act burned her more. She had to contact Angel soon. But how to do it safely? Every step felt so risky. Battered by four crises at once, Istana Negara tried to survive under VP Pradipta's temporary leadership. Reza Satria fought on the front line, bearing the heaviest burden, without realizing there was an enemy in disguise beside him. Nisa Farha was trapped in hiding, planning a desperate step. Istana Negara, Jakarta VVIP Hospital, Reza Satria Group Office

Reza's days were now split into three equally soul-draining battlefields: First Battlefield: The Hospital. Visiting Alex was his top priority, but also his deepest source of pain. Then she began speaking in a gentle tone, “I know Mas Reza must be strong. But don't forget, Mas Reza is also just human. It's okay to feel tired, to feel sad. Don't bottle everything up alone.
