14: Still in the Second Week Since Nisa's 'Illness'
Nisa's Hiding Place, Senen, Central Jakarta

That cramped rented house in a narrow Senen alley became both cocoon and prison for Nisa Farha. Its damp, moldy walls seemed to crawl closer each day, its low ceiling seeming to press on her chest. The single window in the front room she always kept tightly closed with a dull cloth curtain left by previous occupants, afraid of some foreign eye peeking, though the chance of the President of the Republic of Indonesia hiding in a place like this was nearly zero. Daytime felt hot and stuffy, nighttime felt cold and too quiet, only broken by the sound of rats in the attic or the roar of a motorbike occasionally passing in the front alley.

This place was so far different from Istana Negara's grandeur, from the air-conditioned office with green garden views, from the warm and comfortable private pavilion where she used to share stories with Reza at day's end. Here, she was alone. Truly alone. Her old phone she only turned on occasionally to monitor news briefly or send a short anonymous message to the one secret contact she'd tried hard to build (a former junior volunteer now working at a telecommunications company, whom she hoped could help her trace something without too many questions). Her daily food was packed rice from the nearest warteg she bought quietly when it was already dark, eaten on a rickety table accompanied by a bottle of mineral water.

Amid this solitude and such contrasting condition, Nisa's thoughts often drifted far into the past. To the times of her struggle pioneering the path to the peak of power she now so ironically achieved. Sleepless nights no longer because of state burden or political intrigue, but haunted by existential questions: what was all that sacrifice she'd once made for, if it ended up like this?

She remembered her youth. Times when her peers were busy finding boyfriends, hanging out at the newest cafe, or planning dream weddings, Nisa instead was sunk in thick books on constitutional law, political philosophy, and development reports. She spent her weekends not at malls or cinemas, but in heated student discussions, social actions in slum villages, or volunteering at legal aid institutions for the poor. Her free time was poured into sharpening her mind, building her activist network, and formulating her idealism about a better, more just Indonesia.

The first sacrifice was time. Time for youthful fun, time to just relax, time for family. She often missed extended family gatherings, cousins' weddings, or even just dinner with her parents because of an organizational meeting or action she couldn't skip. Her parents, a simple lecturer couple who'd initially hoped Nisa would follow their academic path or at least choose a 'safer' profession for a woman, often complained. “Nis, when will you have time for yourself? When will you start thinking about your personal future?” her mother once asked with an anxious tone. Nisa could only smile and answer that this struggle was also part of her future, the nation's future. An answer that of course didn't fully satisfy her parents' hearts at the time. It took years, it took real proof of achievement, until finally both her parents could accept (though maybe never fully understand) the steep path their only daughter chose. Their blessing felt so costly at the time.

The second sacrifice was friendship. Nisa's social circle slowly narrowed. Her once-close high school or college friends began keeping distance. Some because they felt Nisa was too 'serious,' too 'busy,' no longer having time for just hanging out or light gossip. Others perhaps felt inferior or even a little intimidated by Nisa's 'different' life choice. Reunion invitations came less often, chat group conversations felt increasingly bland. Only a handful of true friends remained, who truly understood Nisa's vision and struggle, who were willing to accept Nisa as she was with all her busyness and 'madness' chasing dreams. One of them, of course, Dinda Larasati. Nisa smiled bitterly remembering her. Dinda… her friend always cheerful, always supportive, who'd even jumped in to help her during the early days of her legislative campaign long ago. Dinda, who now must also be dizzy and sad seeing Nisa's current condition. Nisa felt a little guilty for not having contacted Dinda at all since she disappeared. But how could she? Too risky.

The third sacrifice was personal comfort and security. Choosing the path of politics and activism meant being ready to live in uncertainty, ready to face intimidation, subtle terror, or even physical threat from parties feeling disturbed by her idealism. Nisa remembered well the early times she began being vocal criticizing local government policy or exposing small-scale corruption practice. Her car tires were once deflated, her rented house once had stones thrown at it, she was once followed by an unknown person after a night discussion. All that she faced with her head held high, driven by the conviction that what she fought for was truth.

And the biggest sacrifice was perhaps fragments of herself. Her idealism sometimes made her look rigid or stubborn in others' eyes. Her focus on big goals sometimes made her neglect small things important in personal relationships. She had to learn to build a thick wall of self-defense to protect her heart from disappointment and betrayal inevitable in the political world. Bit by bit, the once-innocent, laughter-filled Nisa perhaps eroded, replaced by a more measured, more watchful, more “presidential” figure of Nisa Farha.

All those sacrifices she made consciously, with conviction that her goal was noble. She wanted to bring change, wanted to prove women could lead, wanted to build a better Indonesia for future generations. And she succeeded. She reached the highest peak of power in this country. She was loved by her people. She succeeded in passing important policy like the Family Readiness Bill now beginning to be felt beneficial.

But now… all that felt like dust amid the slander storm destroying her. The honor she'd guarded so desperately was now torn apart by a cheap fabricated video. Her integrity as a leader was accused full of conflict of interest. Her family, Reza and Alex, who should be her safest harbor, were instead dragged into becoming targets of vicious attack. And she herself now had to hide in this slum place like a criminal, isolated, afraid, and feeling betrayed (by whom, she didn't know).
What was all that sacrifice for? That bitter question echoed again. Was the price of an idealism really this expensive? Did the peak of power actually bring her to her lowest point as a human being?

Nisa stared at the damp wall before her, tears flowing without her realizing. Despair briefly gripped her again. Maybe it was better she just gave up? Come out of hiding, face the legal process (even though she was innocent), then resign from her position? Maybe that way, the attack on Reza and Alex would stop? Maybe she could go back to living peacefully, far from this cruel intrigue?

But then, another image passed. The image of ordinary people's faces she'd once met on her field visits, looking at her full of hope. The image of domestic violence victim women's faces sending her thank-you letters after the Family Readiness Bill passed. The image of Alex's face… her son whose future was now threatened by her enemies' cunning trap.

No. She mustn't give up. Giving up meant letting those slanderers win. Giving up meant betraying all the sacrifices she'd once made. Giving up meant abandoning the hope of millions who believed in her. And most importantly, giving up meant leaving her own son alone facing that vicious accusation.

A mother's instinct, a fighter's instinct, rose again within her. That pain and despair slowly turned into cold anger and burning resolve. She might have fallen, been severely wounded, isolated. But she hadn't lost. Her enemies had underestimated her. They thought by attacking her family and honor, they could destroy her. They were wrong. That very attack now gave her the strongest reason to rise and fight back.

She wiped her tears with the back of her hand. She rose from the cold floor, walking toward the rickety table where her old phone lay. She had to contact Angel soon. Right now. Whatever the risk. She needed an ally. She needed eyes and ears inside the Palace. She needed to start her resistance. This hiding had to end soon, but not by surrendering, rather with a new strategy. Reflecting on her past sacrifices had actually given her strength to face this future still full of uncertainty. That fire lit again.
15: Still in the Second Week Since Nisa's 'Illness'

Jakarta VVIP Hospital. The ivory-white sterile walls of that VVIP treatment room felt increasingly closer each day, imprisoning Alexander Satria in a cage of silence and pain. Physically, he began improving. The stitches on his head had dried, though throbbing dizziness sometimes still struck. His broken left arm was still wrapped in thick cast, hanging stiffly in a sling, but its acute soreness had turned into a more bearable dull ache. However, the invisible wound — the wound in his soul — felt increasingly gaping wide, festering with trauma, fear, and such a thick feeling of abandonment.

Day turned to night in a monotonous cycle only marked by doctor examination schedules, nurse visits to give medicine or change IVs, and painful initial physiotherapy sessions. Outside that medical routine, Alex mostly spent his time staring blankly toward the window showing a sliver of Jakarta's tall buildings, or sometimes staring at his room's white ceiling, letting his mind drift in a labyrinth of bad memories and anxiety about the future.

Every time he tried closing his eyes, that terrifying image came back. Flashes of his fierce argument with Vania in the car. That girl's hysterical scream. Vania's hand movement grabbing the wheel. The ear-splitting screech of tires. The hard collision crushing metal and bone. Then Vania's deathly pale, lifeless face beside him. Sometimes he woke gasping with cold sweat, his heart pounding as if he'd just experienced that accident again.

Then there was the fact of Vania's pregnancy. That news was like a second atomic bomb destroying the remains of his mental defense. Pregnant? How could that be? Alex kept repeating his denial in his heart, then voicing it in frustration to his lawyer, to the nurse, even to his room's wall while alone. He was as certain as certain could be he wasn't the father of that fetus. Their relationship hadn't gone that far. But who would believe it? The autopsy result became 'undeniable proof' in the world's eyes, and his denial only made him look increasingly guilty.

He missed his mother. So much…, so much…, missed her…. He imagined his mother's warm embrace, her calm voice that could always ease Alex's panic since childhood. His mother would surely believe him. His mother would surely know he couldn't possibly do something that cruel. But what Alex knew, his mother was 'ill.' Severely ill, his father said, needing total rest and couldn't be disturbed at all, even by a brief phone call. Alex tried to understand, but the feeling of disappointment and abandonment he couldn't push away. Why did his mother have to be ill exactly when he needed her most? It felt like fate was cruelly toying with him.

His father, Reza, did come visit every day. But that visit felt different. His father looked so tired, so pressured, his eyes conveying an unspoken heavy burden. They did talk, but their conversation felt awkward. Reza mostly asked about Alex's physical condition, about what the doctor said, about Alex's needs at the hospital. He assured Alex the best lawyer team was working, that he'd do everything for Alex. But Alex felt there was distance between them. His father looked busy with his phone, taking important calls about business or whatever. His father no longer had time to just sit quietly beside him, listen to his fear, or maybe cry with him.

“The lawyer said, police will soon conduct further examination once the doctor allows,” Reza said one afternoon, sitting in the chair beside Alex's bed, his eyes on his tablet screen containing some report.
Alex just stayed silent looking out the window.

“Do you… remember other details about that incident, son?” Reza asked again, this time looking at Alex, trying to sound patient. “Anything, however small, could help the lawyer build your defense.” Alex shook his head slowly. “I've told everything I remember, Dad.” His voice sounded flat. He was tired of continuously repeating that terrifying story.
Reza let out a long sigh. “Dad knows this is hard. But you have to be strong. Just tell it as it is to the investigator later. The truth will surely be revealed.”

Alex smiled bitterly inwardly. Truth? Did truth still matter if everyone had already judged him? Including his own father, maybe? Even though his father said he believed him, Alex felt his father also held doubt. The same doubt his mother might also feel if she were here. This feeling made him feel increasingly alone.

He remembered the times before all this chaos happened. His parents were indeed always busy. President and successful businessman. Alex was used to their packed schedule, to their absence in many important moments of his teenage years. He often felt like a satellite orbiting far from his parents' twin suns. He had everything materially, but often felt lacking in emotional connection. Maybe… maybe his closeness with Vania some time ago was also because of that? Because he was looking for a figure who could give him full attention, who could make him feel 'important'? That thought added a layer of guilt within him. Had he unconsciously given Vania false hope because of his own need?

Meetings with his legal team also brought no relief. They did look professional and competent, but their questions felt so cold and piercing. They dissected every detail of Alex's story, looking for inconsistency, forcing him to recall painful moments again. They explained how difficult Alex's position was with Vania's pregnancy fact giving a 'strong motive.' They presented worst-case scenarios if their defense failed. Instead of feeling helped, Alex actually felt increasingly judged and desperate. Even a visit from Auntie Dinda — his mother's always kind friend — didn't comfort him much. Dinda came several times, bringing teen magazines or comics Alex liked, trying to invite him to talk about light things. She always appeared with a gentle smile and encouraging words. “Alex has to get well soon, okay. Auntie and Dad are very worried. Your mom must also be very sad if she knew Alex was like this,” she once said while gently stroking Alex's head. Alex could only reply with a thin smile. Auntie Dinda's attention did feel sincere, but Alex was too sunk in his own world to truly feel it. He just wanted his mother here.

Days passed in a fog of sadness, fear, and loneliness. Alex Satria, the president's son who once lived in privilege and spotlight, now lay injured — physically and mentally — in a hospital room that felt like a prison cell, becoming the main suspect in a tragedy he believed wasn't his fault, abandoned by his 'ill' mother, and feeling increasingly distant from his father burdened by problems. He was truly alone facing the darkest nightmare of his life. And he didn't know, when or how this nightmare would end.

Istana Negara, Jakarta

The pressure at Istana Negara now felt like it had a new epicenter: Vice President Pradipta Angkasa's office. That usually calm senior politician who mostly worked behind the scenes now had to stand under the brightest spotlight, carrying out presidential duties in the most abnormal situation, while guarding the biggest secret that could shake the republic. Every day was an extraordinary balancing test between running the wheels of government, deflecting political attack, and maintaining the lie about President Nisa Farha's condition. That morning, Pradipta had just finished a tense virtual meeting with coalition party chairmen. That meeting was dominated by one topic: uncertainty. When would President Nisa recover? Was her 'illness' permanent? What was the coalition's strategy facing the election if Nisa couldn't run again? Those questions were thrown with polite but insistent tone. Pradipta answered with his best diplomacy, repeating the official narrative about Nisa's condition 'showing progress but needing time,' while assuring the government remained solid under his control. However he knew, the party leaders' patience had its limits. The presidential candidate registration deadline drew closer.

Anton was one of the few people at the Palace who knew the truth about Nisa and now became Pradipta's right hand managing the internal crisis. “Whispers about finding an alternative candidate are getting louder.”

Pradipta let out a long sigh, massaging his forehead. “I know, Ton. But we can't rush. We have to give time for Pak Reza and the team to find Madam President. If we hastily announce another candidate now, that's the same as betraying Madam President.” His loyalty to Nisa remained strong, but he was also aware of his responsibility to the state and coalition.

Pressure didn't only come from within the coalition. Hardiman Suryo and the opposition camp increasingly aggressively exploited the situation. Every day there was some new statement in media questioning Nisa's condition, demanding medical evidence, or mocking VP Pradipta's performance. Hardiman even openly proposed forming a House Special Committee to “evaluate the health condition and ability to carry out the President's duties.” A cunning political maneuver clearly aimed at further discrediting Nisa and her government.

“We have to respond to this special committee issue carefully, Mr. Vice President,” Angel Marina advised in the next coordination meeting also attended by Reza Satria (who took time to come before returning to the hospital). “We mustn't look panicked or defensive.”

Reza, looking increasingly tired and pressured, added, “Our main focus remains Alex. The legal team is preparing pretrial arguments if suspect status is truly established. We mustn't be distracted by Hardiman's maneuver.”

Pradipta nodded in agreement. “Right. We respond to that special committee issue according to procedure, but don't let it divert our energy from the main priority: finding Madam President and defending Alex.” He looked at Reza with concern. “How's Alex's condition today, Pak Reza?”

“Still the same, Mr. Vice President. Mostly silent. The medical team says his physical is far better, but his psychological…” Reza couldn't continue. Thinking of his son alone facing that nightmare felt heart-wrenching.

Amid all this pressure and despair, Angel Marina began feeling something was off, beyond just an ordinary series of political crises. Her instinct and years of closeness with Nisa told her there was a deeper oddity behind all this. Why did attacks come one after another so coordinated? Why did Zidan have to be killed right before Nisa met him? Why could Nisa, a president usually so logical and strong, panic so much she fled?

Angel knew she couldn't just sit idle waiting for Nisa to be found or waiting for this crisis to resolve itself. Driven by her loyalty to Nisa and strong desire to uncover the truth, Angel decided to start her own small 'investigation,' quietly and very carefully, without a specific target at first. She just wanted to find facts, find anomalies, find the missing puzzle pieces.

She began by reviewing all intelligence reports and media analysis that had come in since the Nisa-Zidan video scandal first appeared. She tried mapping its spread pattern, looking for possible initial sources or accounts most instrumental in its amplification. She also asked the Palace's cyber team (with the excuse of ordinary cybersecurity research) to try re-analyzing that video's metadata with more sophisticated techniques, looking for any digital trace however small that might have been missed.

Next, she tried quietly finding out more about Zidan Hidayat. Who were his business colleagues? Did he have enemies? What were his activities in the weeks before he was killed? Angel used her access to several public databases and her contact network carefully, trying to build Zidan's profile without raising suspicion. She found Zidan had just divorced, his financial condition seemed ordinary, and there was no criminal record or serious legal problem in the past. Everything seemed 'normal,' which actually made Angel feel even stranger. Why was Zidan chosen as the target?

She also tried reconstructing the day's events when Nisa disappeared and Zidan was found dead. She reviewed the Palace's security log (which showed nothing suspicious related to Dinda or anyone), Nisa's last communication records (which also seemed normal before her 'morning walk'), and the police's initial report from Zidan's crime scene (which was very minimal in information because of its confidential handling). Everything seemed to hit a dead end. No clear lead.

One afternoon, as Angel was sunk in her analysis in her office, Dinda Larasati came in bringing a cup of warm tea. “Working overtime again, Ngel?” she greeted friendly as usual. “I brought chamomile tea so you can relax a little. You look really tired.”

“Oh, Mbak Dinda, thanks so much,” Angel answered with a tired smile, accepting the tea. “Yeah, lots of work piled up.” She still saw Dinda as Nisa's sincere friend, who was also worried and trying to help in her own way, including giving moral support to the Palace team working hard. “Any developments about Nisa?” Dinda asked carefully, sitting in the chair before Angel's desk.
Angel shook her head slowly. “Nothing yet, Mbak. We're all still trying and praying.”

Dinda let out a long sigh, her eyes looking glistening. “I'm so worried about Nisa. Poor her, alone out there… if she's really… well, if she's really not at the Palace,” she said softly, as if sharing Angel's and Reza's anxiety. “I hope she's okay, Ngel. And I hope all this vicious slander gets uncovered soon.”

“Amen, Mbak Dinda. Amen,” Angel replied earnestly, feeling a little comforted by Dinda's sincere sympathy. Not the slightest thought crossed her mind that the woman before her was one of the keys to all the puzzles she was trying to solve.

Angel's investigation was still at its earliest stage, gathering crumbs of information without clear direction. Meanwhile, political pressure on VP Pradipta kept rising, Alex's case remained stagnant, and Reza Satria kept fighting amid the storm hitting his family. Time kept passing, and the big secret behind the Palace's walls felt increasingly hard to maintain.
17: Entering the Fourth Week Since Nisa's 'Illness'
Nisa's Hiding Place, Senen, Central Jakarta

Days passed in a suffocating monotonous cycle in the cramped Senen rented house. Day turned to night without noticing the difference inside the room always dim, closed by dull curtains. Her old phone with anonymous prepaid SIM proved almost useless. As if Zidan's death was deliberately left to settle into mystery, while Nisa — the key witness most likely to reveal something — was trapped helpless.

She tried re-analyzing her traumatic memory at Zidan's apartment. Looking for odd details that might have been missed. Nisa shook her head hard, trying to expel that bad thought, especially about Dinda, her friend. No, she mustn't think badly of them without evidence. But that uncertainty tormented her. Media kept cornering him, bringing up Vania's pregnancy fact again as the main motive. Nisa saw an interview clip with Alex's lawyer who looked struggling to give a strong defense argument. Her heart screamed wanting to shout defending her son, telling the world Alex was innocent, that this was all a trap! But she couldn't. She was trapped here.

Then news about the political situation. VP Pradipta Angkasa looked increasingly pressured. His statements about Nisa's 'health' condition grew increasingly normative and unconvincing. Hardiman Suryo attacked increasingly boldly, demanding evidence, even threatening to use the House's right of inquiry. Coalition parties were reported to have started closed meetings discussing 'worst-case scenarios.' Nisa knew, her time was almost up. If she didn't soon appear with evidence clearing her name and exposing this conspiracy, her position as president would truly be over, and the lie her team built to protect her would actually become a boomerang destroying them all.

Hunger she sometimes no longer felt, replaced by nausea from stress and meager food. Her sleep grew increasingly worse. Her body felt weak, her energy completely drained. She began rarely bathing, her once always neatly styled hair now tangled and unkempt. She stared at her reflection in the rusty bathroom mirror. A foreign figure stared back. Sunken eyes, gaunt cheeks, dull skin, a gaze full of fear and despair. Where had the old Nisa Farha gone? The strong, smart, confident president? Was this fragile woman in the mirror herself now? One night, as heavy rain poured over Jakarta, creating a frightening rumbling sound on the rented house's tin roof, Nisa reached her lowest point. She ran out of cash. Her last food supply was just a packet of instant noodles. Her old phone ran out of credit and its battery was dying. She felt feverish, maybe from exhaustion or malnutrition. She curled up on a thin damp kapok mattress, shivering cold yet hot, feeling so small, so helpless, so alone in the universe.

Tears flowed without her being able to hold them back anymore. Not tears of anger or ordinary sadness, but tears of total despair. She'd failed. Failed to protect herself, failed to protect Reza, failed to protect Alex. All her past sacrifices felt in vain. All her idealism felt naive. Maybe her enemies were right. Maybe she really wasn't fit to be at this peak of power. Maybe she really was just a weak woman who should just manage a household.

The thought of giving up came again with full force. Get out of here, surrender to police, admit her 'mistake' (though she was innocent), then let the legal process run. Let her be imprisoned, impeached, humiliated. Maybe that way, this torment would end? Maybe the attack on Reza and Alex would stop once she was 'sacrificed'?
She sobbed in the darkness, releasing all the pain, fear, and exhaustion buried for weeks. She felt truly defeated.

However, amid her sobbing, at the nadir of her despair, an awareness slowly emerged. An awareness born not from strength, but actually from acknowledging her own weakness. She couldn't do this alone. She was wrong to think she could uncover a conspiracy this big by herself with only recklessness and paranoia as capital. She needed help. She needed someone she could trust. But who? Reza? She loved Reza too much to drag him further into this danger, especially since Reza already bore such a heavy burden. Dinda? Her friend was indeed very kind, but this Zidan case… it felt too personal to involve Dinda. Besides, Dinda had no access or capacity to conduct investigation at this level. Anton Prasetya? Professional, smart, but Nisa didn't feel personally close enough to entrust her life-or-death secret.

Then… Angel Marina. That name just appeared. Angel. Her quiet personal assistant, very efficient, super loyal, and extraordinarily smart. Angel who for years had been her shadow, knowing almost all her little secrets, arranging her life schedule, even sometimes able to read her mind without her needing to speak. Angel who'd proven she could keep even the most personal secret. Angel who at Zidan's apartment looked equally shocked and horrified as Reza. Angel who now must also be struggling to guard her 'illness' secret at the Palace.
Yes. Angel. Maybe Angel was the only person she could fully trust right now. The only person with the capacity, loyalty, and access to help her from within the Palace.

But how to contact her? Using this old phone was too risky. Sending an anonymous email? Could easily be traced or ignored. Nisa thought hard, her usually sharp brain slowly starting to work again after being paralyzed by despair. She remembered something. A super-secret emergency communication channel they'd once prepared together years ago when Nisa first took office, only for extreme unimaginable crisis situations. An encrypted email address with a special code only the two of them knew. Did Angel still remember it? Was that channel still safe?

This was the last gamble. If Angel didn't respond, or worse, if that channel had already been tapped by the enemy… it would be the end of her story. But if it worked… this could become a turning point in her struggle. With hands trembling from fever and thin hope, Nisa rose from her mattress. She found remaining strength, turned on the old laptop left by previous occupants (which fortunately still worked), and tried accessing that secret email account using a neighbor's internet connection whose signal she'd managed to 'steal.'
She typed a short message, just a few code words they'd once agreed on. No name, no explanation. Just that code. Then, with her heart pounding fast, she pressed 'send.'

Message sent. Now she could only wait. Waiting for a reply from the one person who might become her savior, or waiting for total destruction if her hope was in vain. At her lowest point, Nisa Farha finally admitted she needed help, and she'd just taken the riskiest step to reach it.

No longer just Nisa's hunch or paranoia.

Nisa closed her laptop with mixed feelings. Relieved for successfully contacting Angel and no longer alone. But also horrified imagining the possibility that the real traitor was someone who'd stood so close beside her all this time. This was just the first step. The road was still long and full of danger. But he quickly pushed it aside. He understood Nisa must have a reason. Most importantly, Nisa was safe and they now had a communication channel.

Everything ended within minutes that felt like an eternity. Alex was successfully rescued without additional injury. Pradipta Angkasa and Hardiman Suryo were captured alive.

A few days later, Indonesia calmed again, but with a shocking new understanding. Nisa Farha's second State Address within a week was watched by almost all Indonesian people. This time, she stood at the Palace podium accompanied by Reza and Alex (whose arm was still casted but his face showed relief).

With a calm but authoritative voice, Nisa thoroughly exposed the whole vicious conspiracy masterminded by her own Vice President, Pradipta Angkasa, who'd exploited Hardiman Suryo's and Dinda Larasati's ambition and weakness. She presented evidence of video fabrication, Zidan's murder, exploitation of Vania's tragedy, up to the attempted hostage-taking of Alex. She also apologized to the Indonesian people for the 'lie' about her illness, explaining it was an emergency step to protect herself and uncover the truth. The Indonesian people responded with an overflow of extraordinary sympathy, support, and admiration. Pradipta's betrayal was indeed shocking, but Nisa's steadfastness facing the storm and her success uncovering the conspiracy actually further cemented her image as a strong, integrity-driven leader. Support for her second term became unstoppable.

The legal process ran fast and transparent. Pradipta, Hardiman, Zidan's assassins, Auntie Widya, the rogue mechanic, Pak Jono, and everyone involved were given heavy sentences according to their respective roles. Dinda Larasati, as a key witness, got a far lighter sentence.

At the Palace's private pavilion, a few weeks later, Nisa, Reza, and Alex sat together in the back garden, enjoying a bright afternoon. Those physical and inner wounds might need a long time to fully heal, but their bond as a family felt stronger than before. They'd passed through hell together and succeeded in coming out as winners.

Nisa looked at the blue sky. The road was still long. Her responsibility as President was still great. But now she felt lighter. She'd proven that truth and justice, however hard to fight for, would ultimately win. A new dawn had truly broken for her, for her family, and for Indonesia.
